ety.text: From Middle English daunger (“power, dominion, peril”), from Anglo-Norman dangier, from Old French dangier, alteration of Old French dongier (due to association with Latin damnum (“damage”)) from Vulgar Latin *dominiārium (“authority, power”) from Latin dominus (“lord, master”). Displaced native Old English frēcennes.

senses.d: Exposure to likely harm; risk of death or serious injury.
ex: There's plenty of danger in the desert.
Danger is a good teacher, and makes apt scholars.

senses.d: An instance or cause of likely serious harm.
ex:
1st September 1884, William Gladstone, Second Midlothian Speech
Two territorial questions […] unsettled […] each of which was a positive danger to the peace of Europe.

senses.d: Mischief.
ex: We put a Sting in him, / That at his will he may doe danger with.

senses.d: The stop indication of a signal (usually in the phrase "at danger").
ex: The north signal was at danger because of the rockslide.

senses.d: Ability to harm; someone's dominion or power to harm or penalise. See in one's danger, below.
ex: You stand within his danger, do you not?
Covetousness of gains hath brought [them] in danger of this statute.

senses.d: Liability.
ex: Thou shalt not kyll. Whosoever shall kyll, shalbe in daunger of iudgement.

senses.d: Difficulty; sparingness; hesitation.
ex: They of Coloyne made grete daunger to lete passe the oost thrughe the Cite at brydge.
I made daunger of it a while at first, but afterward beyng persuaded by them..I promised to do as they would haue me.

senses.d: A contemptible person, especially one seen as perverted or mentally ill.
ex: Pineapple and pizza. ONLY JOKING YOU FUCKING DANGER.

senses.d: To claim liability.
To imperil; to endanger.
ex: The sides o'th' world may danger. Much is breeding

senses.d: To run the risk.

Inherited from Old French peril, from Vulgar Latin *periclu(m), syncopated form of Latin perīculum.

Inherited from Old Galician-Portuguese perigoo, probably a semi-learned word from Latin perīculum (“danger”). Compare Galician perigo and Spanish peligro.

phr: a danger foreseen is half avoided

senses.d: A person who dances, usually as a hobby, an occupation, or a profession.

ety.text: From Middle English daungerous (“difficult, severe, domineering, arrogant, fraught with danger”), dangerous, from Anglo-Norman [Term?], from Old French dangereus (“threatening, difficult”), from dangier. Equivalent to danger + -ous. Displaced native Old English frēcne.

senses.d: Full of danger.
ex: Railway crossings without gates are highly dangerous.

senses.d: Causing danger; ready to do harm or injury.

Middle English dauncen English dance Inherited from Middle English dauncen, borrowed from Anglo-Norman dauncer, from Vulgar Latin *dantiāre, of uncertain origin. Displaced native Old English sealtian, Old English frīcian, and partially displaced Old English hlēapan (“to leap, dance, run”, whence modern leap). Doublet of danza.
Related to dancy, dancetté, French danché.

senses.d: A sequence of rhythmic steps or movements usually performed to music, for pleasure or as a form of social interaction.
ex: I do a dance when she plays the drums!
He does the Gangnam Style dance with his friends in school.

senses.d: A social gathering where dancing is the main activity.
ex: The dance we had in August 2008 is one of the greatest moments of my life!

senses.d: The art, profession, and study of dancing.
A piece of music with a particular dance rhythm.
A battle of wits, especially one commonly fought between two rivals.
ex: So how much longer are we gonna do this dance?

senses.d: Any strenuous or difficult movement, action, or task.
A repetitive movement used in communication between worker honey bees.
To move with rhythmic steps or movements, especially in time to music.
ex: I danced with her all night long.
These drum beats are making me dance!

senses.d: To leap or move lightly and rapidly.
ex: His eyes danced with pleasure as he spoke. She accused her political opponent of dancing around the issue instead of confronting it.
And woods along the banks are waving high, / Whose shadows in the glassy waters dance,

senses.d: To perform the steps to.
ex: Have you ever danced the tango?

senses.d: To cause to dance, or move nimbly or merrily about.
ex: Thy grandsire loved thee well; / Many a time he danced thee on his knee.

senses.d: To make love or have sex.
ex: You make me feel like dancing.

senses.d: To make a repetitive movement in order to communicate to other worker honey bees.
To kick and convulse from the effects of being hanged.

Or, a dance gules, in chief 3 lions' faces sable.
